records.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
records.author: FabCH
records.storyText:
I have been researching what the ultimate diff tool would look like, based on actual diffs in open source repositories.

OmniDiff can diff: code (25 languages), config, images, PDFs, archives, cursors, fonts...

It's fast. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in under 100ms, on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s.

It's open source. AGPLv3.

It's based on real diffs. I looked at the 7400 repositories that are listed in Gentoo packages, sampled 2000 diffs and solved them manually to get a good understanding of what is needed, before putting together the diff pipelines for each content type. Incidentally, this also forms the basis of the CI pipeline, so the robustness of the codebase is quite high.

I'm still developing it. It's v0.3.0 at this time. But I have been using it daily as my git difftool for months now, and it works well.

AI Disclosure: Yes, I do use AI. No, I do not vibecode.

records.title: Show HN: Jointter – A daily word puzzle using dots and lines
records.author: proy87
records.storyText:
Hello everyone. I’m a mathematician by training, and I love mathematical and logical puzzles and brain-teasers. Inspired by popular games like Sudoku and Wordle, I decided to come up with an engaging game of my own.

As it turns out, that’s not so easy! I had a few ideas, but beyond the core mechanics, a game also needs to be interesting and easy to explain — after all, nobody (including me) wants to spend a long time reading through rules.

Let’s start with the concept, which came to me quite spontaneously: what if we represented letters like the digits on a digital clock — using lines, with dots at the points where those lines intersect? For instance, the letter "E" would consist of four lines and six dots — three at the intersections and three at the ends of the lines.

It turns out that every letter of the Latin alphabet can be represented this way (with a minor caveat) using three rows of dots connected by some lines. This immediately presented a challenge: how do you represent O-shaped parts, like those found in "B", "O", or "R"? I decided not to use O-shapes, an use onl rectangles/squares. This "alphabet" is always displayed below the game board, so the player can see the letters.

The goal of the game is simple: you are presented with three rows of dots and a set of lines, and you have to figure out the word. A great feature of the game is that it’s possible to deduce the word in a single turn — all the necessary information is right there on the board, allowing you to arrive at the answer with certainty. And what if you can’t figure it out on the first try? You can enter a guess, much like in Wordle: if the lines from the entered word are part of the target word, they turn green; if not, they turn red. The same applies to the dots. As you play, more and more lines gradually appear...

Why provide some lines at the start? To uniquely identify a specific word — or a small set of words — from the dictionary. For example, you could select a configuration of lines that corresponds to only one word, like "RADIO", or perhaps to just two possible words, such as "WEIGH" and "WRONG".

The rules seem clear, but the mechanics — not so much. There are dots on the board; when I enter a word, I realize there aren't enough dots. What should I do? Initially, if the target word had 5 letters, I allowed users to enter 4- or 5-letter guesses, but that just confused players. So, I came up with a different solution: adding red dots for dots that aren't part of the target word.

Another drawback is that the game is somewhat skewed. Since letters are processed from left to right, the first letters are revealed more frequently than the last ones.

Then there’s the game design itself: should the target words be 5 letters long, or 6? Should a single board allow for multiple possible answers (like "WEIGH" and "WRONG"), or should it be limited to one — or perhaps more than two? Should the difficulty increase from Monday to Sunday? Currently, it’s set up this way: Monday is the easiest (a few 3-letter words), while Sunday is the hardest (more than two 7-letter words).

The tech stack is simple: I use Flask for the backend and Python for the algorithms; I wrote the algorithms myself. While the JS, HTML, and CSS were created with the help of AI.

I’d love for you to test the game and share what you like, what you don’t, and what could be improved.

Specifically, I’d like to know:

1. Is the game and its goal clear?

2. Is it fun to play, and what could be improved?

3. Would you share it with your friends?

I welcome any constructive criticism.

You can find the game at https://www.jointter.com/

It’s free and requires no registration.

Thank you very much.

Hi everyone :)

After almost a year of fighting windmills, I am proud to say I built sweet-search, a local code search tool for Claude Code, Codex and Opencode.

It consists of 6 tools: hybrid search with late interaction reranking, my version of grep, and others. It also has GPU accelerated indexing (for embedding and late interaction models) and low footprint incremental indexing.

Some highlights: 1. The ANN kernel is custom and very competitive with FAISS and USearch. 2. The custom MaxSim kernel is 1.4–7.3× faster than NumPy and PyTorch (reranking on CPU). 3. My hybrid-search tool is SOTA on M2CRB and zero-shot SOTA on CoSQA. 4. My custom grep tool is 2.46x faster e2e than ripgrep and ranks hits in a specific way (inspired by Sainte-Laguë).

Here is the promo video I built with fframes and Opus 5.5: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lJzgXRQprs4

Would love to hear your opinions, Marko :)

records.title: Show HN: Shroom – screen recording and sharing, your own Cloudflare, 10M setup
records.author: _bagrat
records.storyText:
Some months I needed to record and share a single 30-minute demo, but in other months I only needed a few 2-minute quick videos. Paying $18/month didn't justify. So I had to build it myself.

Shroom is a free, open source (MIT) screen recording and sharing app for Mac, hosted in your own Cloudflare account. Install with one line (or with your AI agent) and follow a guided setup for about 10 minutes, a few clicks (create a token, add a card to enable storage on Cloudflare).

With Cloudflare's free tier, up to about 3 hours of recorded videos cost you nothing. After that, it is still cheap - use the slider at https://shroom.am to see the approximate storage costs.

Shroom auto-deletes stale videos (old, unwatched) to keep your storage consumption low. Pin important videos to keep them from being deleted.

Invite your teammates with a single link, they don't need a Cloudflare account. Their videos go into your storage. You only pay for storage, no matter how many people you invite.

It comes with an editor, but you can also cut as you record. If you make a mistake, just say "shroom cut" while recording and continue. After you stop the slipped sentence will be cut for you. It will also add chapters and captions to your video using AI, again, all running in your Cloudflare.

Github: https://github.com/bagrat/shroom

records.title: Show HN: Learn to beatmatch on Winamp-skinned decks (vibe-coded, desktop only)
records.author: fi3
records.storyText:
## Intro

Given all the token resets in the last few weeks, I decided to try building a fully vibe, and fully one-shotted project (one prompt per feature/bug fix, no reviews, neither human nor indipendent agents, only the ones the agent itself spawns).

That's how bit-cheer https://bit-cheer.com was born, a tool for learning beatmatching that I really wish I had when I started with turntables. The idea is absolutely not new, and if you want to learn beatmatching and want something much more tested and still free, I recommend https://www.beatmatch.pro/.

I needed a somewhat challenging task to see how far I could get with this 100% vibe, one-shotted approach, and I liked the somewhat nostalgic idea of using early 2000s graphics, so bit-cheer reuses Winamp's graphics and elements and can "wear" any Winamp skin.

## No mobile

The app was intentionally designed not to support mobile. I didn't feel like going crazy trying to make Winamp skins work on mobile, and it most likely never will support it.

## Technical details

The web app is written in Elm (with a bit of js, mainly for plumbing and skin rendering) and uses an audio engine written in Rust and compiled to WASM. That's all I know. (I had to ask the agent what it uses npm and js for, and it used for what I was more or less expecting)

What I didn't expect is that, for some reason, it decided not to use elm-test, so the score matcher, which according to the agent needs unit tests, is written entirely in JS. Two other unexpected things are (1) the Comfort/HD feature, which does pixel enhancement and is pretty CPU-heavy, is in js even though Rust/WASM was an option, and (2) the Vite and Elm dependencies are not up to date.

These are the only three issues that came out of a very quick review (literally a handful of questions to the agent). Everything else was done purely as a "user", meaning using the app and giving my feedback to the agent.

Most of the skin rendering was done by Claude with Opus 5.5 Max, while most of the audio engine was done by Astra 6 Ultra. The FE is 50/50.

I find that what I got is a very good result, considering that I give the agent only few high level instructions and then only used the app and reported bug and asked for features.

## The webapp

The webapp offers 5 modes:

* Foundation: you need to match 2 different kicks, and you can see the BPM of each track.

* Loop builder: you need to match 2 complete loops (many instruments, not just a kick), and you can see the BPM (you can build your own loops as well).

* By ear: same as loop builder, but BPMs are hidden.

* Star mode: same as by ear, but BPMs are not constant and you need to keep the tracks aligned.

* Pro decks: you can play actual music, 40 CC tracks or tracks you load from your PC. You can enable star mode here as well to keep things more interesting.

In any mode, you have a coach that will rate your run.

It also offer an 8 lesson learning path an hardwar mixed support (still not tested) and, of course, the skin studio.

## Links

* bit-cheer: https://bit-cheer.com/

* github: https://github.com/Fi3/bit-cheer/

records.title: Show HN: Othismo, a Runtime for Sandboxed Objects
records.author: mamidon
records.storyText:
Othismo is a runtime which has a bunch of sandboxed WASM modules talking to each other + the host environment. It's actually hosting its own website right now at othismo.com.

This is a project that's been percolating in my head for a while, as a vague desire to make a "better" runtime for software development. But it was never particularly clear for me what that would _actually_ look like. In the last month or so, I felt a bit inspired to ask what such a runtime might look like for agentic development.

My hypothesis is that we really can't review 10k+ SLoC pull requests consistently and really understand them. But if we try to have a higher level view of things, we still can't be confident the agent(s) haven't done something stupid and opened a socket or a file somewhere in that 10k+ SLoC.

Therefore we need a very clear demarcation between computation and side effects. In Othismo that takes the shape of the image definition files (.oth) which describe the namespace + various type definitions describing what the interface of an object (should) be. It's somewhat like TypeScript, we don't actually do anything to verify an object conforms to this interface.

I'd love your feedback on the syntax used to define images overall, I feel like it doesn't do a great job giving me a clear notion of the environment lexically. I'm more comfortable about the syntax for describing the behavior of objects, although things like `operator` and `readonly` are really only necessary because I've not done anything to support auth at the protocol layer yet.

You can run the same website hosted at othismo.com with

`git clone git@github.com:mamidon/othismo.git`

`task run:example:static`

You can also play with the namespace interactively with

``` task build:example:static target/debug/othismo shell examples/static/static.rti

# print out the namespace(s) target/debug/othismo --check examples/static/static.rti ```

You'll need rust, task (it's like make), and node+npm.

records.title: Show HN: [Pulse] Thanks to C, I have a project with which I am happy
records.author: xerrs
records.storyText:
I have been dabbling with programming ever since Covid was a thing. And since then I jumped around and programmed a lot of stuff, whether it was Websites, Apps or simple Python programs. Unfortunately, I have never really gotten that "feel", the feel of being useful or something like that. Most of the projects I have done, died out, and the issue was not just that my programs were not reaching anybody, it was also that I felt like I was not learning anything.

Then came C, and I just have to say, that it was probably one of the best decisions I have ever made. I have tried C a lot, once I was 15, 17, and now, 19 years old. This time it stuck with me, and moved me to create my own organization called cherries.works, with the sole focus of creating efficient, open source, free and simple tools for developers.

After more than 5 contributions, issues created, bugs fixed, letting it run on my own homelab for 4-5 hours, I can confidently say, that with the help of C, my biggest project Pulse was made ( https://github.com/cherries-works/pulse ).

I was vacating somewhere and left my laptop at home. I brainstormed a lot about creating this organization during my vacation, and my project Pulse. This is around 6 months ago. And now after 6 months, seeing how well everything turned, really makes me happy.

Might be far-fetched, but as someone who has learned multiple languages, coded in multiple areas, and created (way) too many projects, I can confidently say, that thanks to C, I have a project that actually makes me happy.

Pulse is a simple monitoring tool that does not require you to sign in, or setup anything. You just download it with a single curl command, and run it on your device. I created it because I really dont like the setup hell, or whatever it takes to get a single monitoring tool running, and also because I wanted to learn C, not to mention having a program I control would mean I can add my features I would want (such as quick web hosting, API sharing, JSON formatting, styling etc.). At the end, it really was a win-win for me.

Would mean a lot if devs who are interested could check it out, and point me towards some issues that I could fix, as I feel like the project is reaching a stagnation point. But even then, I am just really happy to look at Pulse, and be able to say, that *I, me* are the one who programmed that.

The port runs on a 32-bit RISC-V CPU at 360 MHz with an 8 MB default PSRAM buffer. It runs 60,000-row TPC-H queries in under a second.

Project home: https://github.com/habedi/duckdb-micro

Benchmarks: https://github.com/habedi/duckdb-micro/blob/main/docs/benchm...

records.title: Show HN: IsSiteDown – Chrome extension to check current site availability
records.author: gin_dev
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I have recently built a small Chrome extension, showing availability of the currently open site. Like you can't open something and want to quickly check, if it is down at all.

It checks HTTP responses, DNS resolution and TLS certificate from the cloud environment.

For a set of well-known sites it also provides information from official status (e.g. Cloudflare, Airbnb etc.), showing short info about latest incidents, if any.

I'm interested in a few things: 1. In which scenarios would you use it? Own sites, general surfing, quick link to official reports? 2. Is it worth to extend this official status part, covering more sites? Which services would you want covered?

records.title: Show HN: Turn websites into audio locally in the browser with WebGPU
records.author: hallh
records.storyText:
I wanted a simple way to listen to articles on the go and found elevenreader. While I think the voices they have are great, I didn't want to bother with an account, a subscription, and yet another service interested in my content habits.

I thought that TTS models and runtimes surely must have reached a point where they can run effectively on a mobile device with WebGPU. Maybe a fully local webapp could be feasible?

Shortly after, I heard about Phonon here on HN and was motivated to spend a weekend with Claude and see what we could come up with :)

The result is:

- A fully local Audiobook/TTS webapp - An optimised Phonon runtime reaching ~4x increase in speed on WebGPU and CPU compared to stock Phonon - Streaming, so the audio starts quickly and continues to generate uninterrupted while the phone is locked - Library with an optional "auto-download" feature, so you can pre-render articles to be listened to later - Fully serverless and local, the bundle is hosted in Cloudflare workers, no backend, no database, no user accounts, no tracking. Only piece of backend logic is a simple proxy to use as fallback for fetching URLs that the browser is unable to fetch b/c of CORS

Depending on your OS version, you may need to enable WebGPU in iOS/Safari settings, Chromium-based browsers in chrome://flags (search for WebGPU and enable both settings), and allow JIT in Site Controls on Vanadium (GrapheneOS).

records.title: Show HN: Muse Zouroboros, gives Muse a software factory
records.author: marlandoj
records.storyText:
Hello HN. I built the Zouroboros workshop on Muse. Together I think they are the most powerful vibecoding workshop tool on the planet today.

I use Muse as my daily assistant. Its pretty awesome until you want it to build using different models or tools. That's where the workshop comes in. If I want to build anything complex or long running jobs that last hours or days, Muse sends it to the workshop.

The workshop itself splits jobs up into pieces and determines which harness is best used for that job. 7 harnesses are installed in all, more can be added. Claude,Hermes,Codex, Gemini are the big players. The workshop routes harnesses and models based on the job.

The workshop itself is more than a harness and model router. Its persistent memory. In fact Zouroboros started out as a memory substrate like SuperMemory but it has since evolved. Memory is the core. The cool part is that memory on the workshop work for any frontend agent like Muse. Snapping them together was frictionless.

The package is on npm in the repo link. There is a community version and a hosted version if true vibecoding builders want to get serious. Solo builders can build with the communnity version or scale up to hosted since Muse has limited resources itself.

Its a rough implementation on the verge of a GTM. I wont lie. I would like to hear how others are vibecoding using Muse and if a workshop would benefit them.

records.title: Show HN: Clawdline – Manage Claude Code/Codex sessions across computers
records.author: sainteye
records.storyText:
I built Clawdline to manage Claude Code and Codex sessions across multiple computers in one place.

It runs on multiple computers (Mac and Linux), and you can see all of your sessions in one list. Each session reports its status (working, completed, or needs attention). You can also manage all your sessions and receive notifications from your phone (web app).

Herdr, T3 Code, and Orca already cover a lot of this space, and there’s overlap.

When I started building Clawdline, I didn't know about Herdr, T3 Code, or Orca. So I built it to fit my own dev workflow. At first, I used Swift to build a Mac app, but I realized that it wouldn't work if I also wanted to support Linux. So I decided to rewrite it in Go. Now it can support both of them.

Main Features:

- Cross Machine Agent Communication: You can ask a root session ("Local") on your Mac to start a new session ("Remote") on a remote Linux machine. Once the remote session finishes its work, it notifies the root ("Local") session.

- Cross Agent Communication: You can use one root session to create tasks need multiple agents. They can communicate with each other through clawdline

- Scheduled Task with Webhook: You can create scheduled tasks and combine them with your service (use webhooks to trigger new agent sessions)

- Board System: tasks control for Feature, Issue, Epic, Refactor, Plan

- Snippet/Playbook: If there are commands you use them very often, snippet can help you

- TODO: lightweight tasks

- Note: Agents can leave notes to you if they need your attention

- Agent Squad: assign role to any task or session

- Archive: you can archive sessions and see it in one place

- Others: Intelligence session naming, Image/Video display, Voice input, Machine monitor, Usage Monitor, Dev Stack Run, Deploy progress monitor...

This project is open source and I have used Claude & Codex to do independent reviews on Clawdline, Herdr, T3 and Orca. (you can find the reviews on the website.)

The work still needs further input and feedback. Hope this helps other developers improve their devs! :)
